A1.justification: Despite the changed title and organization, both PDFs describe the same FedBis/FedBiscuit research. All supplied pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original summarization experiments in Table 1 and Figure 3, QA experiments in Appendix B.1, and generated examples in Appendix B.2.

after.justification: V2 reports original summarization and QA experiments in Tables 1–2, selector-size experiments in Appendix B.3, and generated examples in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The substantive procedure remains CE-based binary-selector training, FedBiscuit warm-up and balanced loss-based clustering, selector aggregation, majority voting, and DPO on generated preferences. V2 adds pseudocode and reorganizes the description; its Appendix A largely preserves v1's FedBis implementation.

E1.justification: V2 adds SafeRLHF prompts as an alternative source for QA alignment, extending training-input coverage beyond Reddit prompts. TL;DR summarization and SHP-based QA remain the principal tasks. The AlpacaEval 2.0 change primarily concerns evaluation protocol; the PDFs do not establish a distinct new evaluation population.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates direct FedAvg and FedDPO fine-tuning baselines in both tasks, whereas v1's summarization comparison used SFT and centralized preference training and its QA comparison used Alpaca-7B. The centralized comparator disappears. The unaligned-model comparison remains, with changed model configurations.

E3.justification: V2 expands generator and selector configurations to Gemma and Qwen, changes QA from 300 clients and 200 rounds to 200 clients and 500 rounds, and increases QA local updates from 10 to 30. QA evaluation changes from Auto-J ratings to AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rates against GPT-4 responses. Summarization drops agreement, best-of-n and rating metrics. LoRA dropout changes from 0 to 0.05 and sampling temperature from 1.0 to 0.7.

E4.justification: V2 adds comparisons of three versus five selectors, selector backbones, Qwen selector sizes, and Reddit versus SafeRLHF prompts. The existing two-versus-four-completion analysis is retained under revised settings. Conversely, v1's training-round trajectory used to investigate reward hacking is removed. Four new qualitative examples replace the two earlier examples.

E5.justification: V1 reports performance point estimates only; v2 Table 2 adds ± quantities to QA win rates. Their statistical meaning, run counts and seeds are unspecified, so this establishes additional uncertainty reporting without establishing repeated training runs or a particular estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The principal results are substantially replaced. V1 Table 1 reports summarization win rates of 80.65% for FedBiscuit and 71.35% for FedBis. Under v2's LLaMA-2 generator/selector configuration, Table 1 instead reports 91.87% for FedBis and 90.84% for FedBiscuit with three selectors. V2 adds extensive QA and selector-size results while removing the earlier selector diagnostics. These are results under changed settings, not directly comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 Section 5 explicitly requires an odd number of selectors to ensure a decisive binary majority vote; v1 did not state this restriction. The optimization objectives, balance constraint, aggregation equations and DPO loss otherwise remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies a theoretical guarantee or proof.

C1.justification: The headline empirical claim shifts from FedBiscuit outperforming FedBis and centralized training to both FedBis and FedBiscuit improving Gemma and LLaMA alignment. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are revised accordingly, while retaining the federated preference-learning framework and benchmark contributions.

C2.justification: V1 explains FedBiscuit's summarization advantage through generalization and delayed reward hacking, and its QA disadvantage through insufficient training. V2 instead attributes FedBis's summarization advantage to limited preference heterogeneity and discusses FedDPO data mismatch, prompt sources and selector capacity. V1's substantive limitations concerning proxy client data, narrow task coverage and inability to represent equal-quality responses are removed. Some new interpretations overgeneralize: the claimed universal baseline degradation conflicts with Table 1's LLaMA-2 FedDPO result.

D1.justification: V2 adds dataset-size and client-distribution statistics, a disclosed SHP token filter, generation limits, an additional QA prompt template and checkpoint-selection information. Hardware changes from two A100 GPUs to one, and v1's promised dataset/code releases are omitted. Documentation remains inconsistent: Section 7.1 specifies three fine-tuning epochs, whereas Appendix B Tables 3–4 specify five.

R1.justification: V2 adds a focused discussion of the already-cited OpenFedLLM's FedDPO approach and distinguishes it through computational, heterogeneity and reward-hacking concerns. Additional citations support on-device models, newer FL background and length-controlled evaluation. The broader RLHF and clustered-FL positioning remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, changes the title and author information, introduces a preliminary section, moves detailed FedBis exposition into Appendix A, and brings QA evaluation into the main text. The experimental narrative and appendix organization are extensively restructured.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. V2 adds a privacy-comparison diagram and algorithm display, redraws the workflow into three steps, restructures result tables, adds dataset and selector-size tables, and consolidates prompts into Figure 4. The training-trajectory plot disappears, and compact example tables become four full-page dialogue figures.

improvement.justification: The direct FedAvg/FedDPO comparisons and selector-size, selector-count and prompt-source analyses provide a more informative empirical assessment than v1's limited comparisons. The net gain is constrained by removal of the centralized comparison, reward-hacking trajectory and substantive limitations. V2 also introduces conflicting training budgets and overstates baseline degradation: Table 1 reports LLaMA-2 FedDPO at 77.02% versus the raw model's 76.79%. These tradeoffs limit the improvement despite the broader evaluation.
